name: Radior

card.summary: Radior was a radium cosmetic line from the 1910s marketed for beauty and a regenerated complexion.

quick.overview:
Radior was a French radium cosmetics brand of the 1910s, sold during the fashion for "radium and beauty". Its pitch was regenerative, anti-aging skin care.

A 1918 advertisement titled "Radium and Beauty" shows the brand. It was one of several brands, alongside Activa, that profited from "microcurietherapy", the idea that tiny radium doses could energise cells.
quick.how: It was sold as consumer creams and similar cosmetics, not as a modern routine. It is not in use today.
quick.risks: Radium is radioactive; the wider radium craze involved documented harms, mainly among dial painters. France restricted radioactive materials to prescription with warning labels in 1937.

lead: Radior was a radium-containing cosmetic line from the 1910s, marketed for beauty and a more youthful complexion.[1][2]

Pharmacist Alexandre Jaboin proposed "microcurietherapy" in the early 1910s, and brands such as Activa and Radior profited from the trend. A 1918 Radior advertisement was titled "Radium and Beauty".[1]
Radium cosmetics were promoted with regenerative and anti-aging claims.[2]

angle.text: Customers used radium creams hoping for rejuvenated skin, as the brand advertised.

paras: Radior and Activa profited from microcurietherapy in the 1910s.[1] Later, Tho-Radia (1932) had radium until 1937, when French rules limited radioactive materials to prescription and required warning labels.[1]

Wikipedia's radium article notes harms from the era are chiefly documented among dial painters, including jaw necrosis, anemia and cancer; the cosmetics themselves are not described as causing documented harm there.[2]
